newsitem.title: USA: Strong U.S. economic data lifts dollar.
newsitem.headline: Strong U.S. economic data lifts dollar.

text.p: The dollar rose moderately against most leading currencies Thursday, bolstered by economic reports that hinted the Federal Reserve might need to hike interest rates next week to keep inflation in check.
The Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, in a widely watched survey of local manufacturers, reported solid increases in two indexes that gauge price pressures.

Further signs that a robust economy might fuel inflationary pressures emerged when the Commerce Department reported that builders broke ground on new homes and apartments in August at the fastest rate in about 2-1/2 years.

The Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed's policy-setting arm, meets Sept. 24. Expectations for an interest rate increase were already in the market, and Thursday's surprisingly strong figures added fuel to the fire.

"That meant that people were starting to look for a Fed rate hike at the next FOMC meeting, which is why the dollar bounced up early on," said Peter Wadkins, a vice president of foreign exchange at Standard Chartered Bank.
Higher interest rates help the American currency by making dollar-denominated deposits more attractive to foreign investors.
In late New York trading, the dollar stood at 1.5136 German marks, up from 1.5090 marks Wednesday. The dollar traded at 109.44 Japanese yen, up from 109.12 yen.
U.S. figures helped the dollar, but solid German economic data also released Thursday failed to boost the mark, causing it to weaken further against the U.S. currency.
A German Ifo economic research institute report showed business confidence improved in August.

Furthermore, German money supply, or M3, which the Bundesbank sees as an important indicator of inflationary trends, unexpectedly grew at an annualized rate of 8.7 percent in August compared with an 8.6 percent rise in July. That was above economists' forecast for growth of about 8.0 percent and marked the first pickup in M3 growth since February.
Typically such figures might be expected to strengthen the mark by diminishing hopes for another decrease in German official interest rates.

"The failure of the mark to benefit from the European news sort of sapped the strength of the mark against the dollar," said Chris Widness, an international economist at Chase Securities Inc. "I think it's because the market is convinced that as long as there is a political will in Europe to proceed with monetary union, it really doesn't matter that much what the economic data are."

Germany and France are spearheading an effort to launch a single European currency in January 1999. A growing belief that this goal will be realised could lessen the mark's status as a safe-haven currency in Europe.

With no other major American economic data due out this week, currency traders are now free to focus on next Tuesday's Fed meeting. Heading into that all-important gathering, the dollar maintains a positive underlying trend, traders said.

"Obviously the interest rate advantage of the dollar is not going to disappear on the 24th (of September)," said Diego Giurleo, a vice president of the Treasury Department at the Royal Bank of Canada. "The only question is, does it get wider?"
In other trading, the British pound fell to $1.5532 Thursday from $1.5615 Wednesday. The dollar rose slightly to 1.2428 Swiss francs from 1.2420 francs but slid to Canadian $1.3705 from C$1.3718.
